for each individual phenomenon possesses its own distinct limits and divisions. 3. The Dharma-realm of the Unobstructed Interfusion of Principle and Phenomena;

for all phenomena with their various divisions are each interfused with the nature of reality, becoming infinitely layered and inexhaustible. On the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no... [text continues]

Receiving a single speck of dust, it is pure of itself without depending on purification. Fourth is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadhātu-avaraṇa-vinirmukta*).

Phenomena possess both defilement and purity, and thus must naturally be distinguished; yet within the realm of phenomena, there is further the distinction between the physical body and the environment.
This refers to the root-body within the realm of pure phenomena. This is because the root-body is formed from the two drops of red and white [semen and ovum] provided by one's parents.
Furthermore, because of the accumulated empty habits from beginningless lifetimes, one purifies them.
Since each of the six sense organs and four limbs has its own laws and its own boundaries, they are therefore called the "Dharmadhātu. When reciting mantras, one should discipline both body and mind.
Visualize the syllables Oṃ and Āḥ at the crown and the navel, representing the perfection of merit and wisdom.
Why is this? Without merit, one cannot possess the primary and secondary marks; without wisdom, one cannot purify remaining defilements.

When merit and wisdom are perfected, internal obstacles are naturally purified and external appearances are naturally adorned. Therefore, one visualizes the syllable Oṃ at the crown and the syllable Āḥ at the navel. As for the crown, it is one...

The head is the foremost part of the body, and the navel is the source of the life-vein (*prāṇa-marma*). If these two places are purified, there will be nothing among the six sense organs or the four limbs that is not purified.

Question: How do these two characters [Oṃ and Āḥ] bring about the two purifications (*dvi-saṃbhāra*)? Answer: The Sūtra states: "The syllable Oṃ is the true principle of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
it is the meaning of the fundamental non-arising of all phenomena. Furthermore, it signifies the three bodies (*tri-kāya*). It is the invisible crown of the head."
Regarding the meaning of the *lakṣaṇa* (marks): it also carries the meaning of the Tathāgata’s marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) and his meritorious virtues.

To visualize it upon the crown of the head is to embody all the aforementioned meanings. As for the syllable *Lam*, the mantra ritual manual states: "This is named the Samādhi of the Jewel Cloud, the Pervasive Illumination of Buddha-Wisdom.
Whether one visualizes or recites it, it causes the three karmas to become entirely pure and purifies all transgressions.
Obstacles will be completely extinguished, and one will be able to accomplish all virtuous deeds. Wherever one dwells, that place shall become entirely pure.
If clothing is impure, it becomes pure clothing; if the body has not been bathed, it becomes as if bathed.
If one seeks purity through water, it is not called true purity; if one purifies by means of these syllables, it is called ultimate purity.
Just as a single grain of elixir transforms iron into gold, so a single syllable of mantra transforms defilement into purity.
As the verse says: The syllable *Lam* is brilliant white, adorned with the bindu. Like a luminous jewel in a topknot, it is placed upon the crown.
This mantra is identical to the Dharmadhātu; immeasurable multitudes of sins are eliminated. In all places touched by impurity, one should...

Add this gateway of letters. The reason for placing these characters at the source of life (*mingyuan*) is that the various sense-faculties will then be fully uprooted and internally clarified, emitting light.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Once one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the consecration mantra (*abhiṣeka-mantra*): because this purifies the vessel-like realm (*bhājanaloka*), it is called "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*).
When reciting the mantra, take scented water with the ring finger of the right hand, sprinkle it into the air, and smear it upon the palm; then, visualize the interior of the maṇḍala.
Externally, all are entirely pure. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "If one world is pure, many worlds are likewise so;
thus it extends until the very limits of space, encompassing the three periods of time, all being equally pure, unmoving, and tranquil.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "According to the purity of one's own mind, so too is the Buddha-land pure."
Regarding the mantra for consecrating flowers and rice: "flower" (*puṣpa*) signifies the meaning of cause; thus, one takes this rice as the cause.
When reciting the mantra, one should visualize it becoming the seed of the light of wisdom, from which clouds of gold, silver, beryl, and so forth are produced.

As for the preliminary consecration, when these are employed, they transform according to one's intention without contradiction. This is precisely what is meant by the saying: "When a craftsman desires excellence..."
This is the meaning of the principle that "in all undertakings, one must first sharpen one's tools.
Regarding the mantra of the bell and pestle: the bell signifies "delight" (*sukha*). Placing it on the left side of the waist symbolizes the "Great Self" (*mahātman*).
This self is not the self conceived through the emotional calculations of ordinary beings; rather, it is the true *ātman*—the permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity—within the Dharmakāya.
The self that is eternally quiescent and extinguished. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

This is precisely the meaning of the "self" (*ātman*). It is like a bell: empty yet capable of resonance; when stimulated, it immediately responds, perfectly harmonizing with the Buddha-mind and gladdening the capacities of all beings.
Thus, the bell speaks of compassion, manifesting the virtue of the self. By shaking it, one delights the minds of both sentient beings and Buddhas.

Thus it is. The *mudgara* (hammer) signifies the meaning of manifesting majestic power (*vibhūti*) and also symbolizes the five wisdoms (*pañca-jñāna*). Turning the fist outward is to show it to sentient beings.
Regarding the symbolism of the five wisdoms: it is because wisdom can crush and destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*) and subdue the armies of Māra.
When reciting the mantra, one should hold flowers and rice grains with the right hand and sprinkle them over the bell and hammer while performing the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ. This is called the Three-Syllable Dhāraṇī Mantra. In all ritual practices, one should empower everything with this mantra;
thus, all will attain firm, vast, and inexhaustible utility. The Yoga Mahātantra Sūtra states:
"By virtue of the empowering power of upholding this syllable Oṃ, even if one's visualization is not perfected,"
Within the ocean-like assemblies of all Buddhas and the ocean-like clouds of offerings, one truly achieves perfection.

This is because it is established by the truth of the Buddhas and through the natural law (*dharmatā*). By reciting the syllable *A*, one destroys all karmic obstacles and afflictions, attaining all desired joys and becoming equal to all Buddhas.
One transcends the hosts of noble ones and Māras, such that they can no longer create obstructions; thus, one is worthy of receiving [offerings].

Throughout all worlds, even vast offerings, through the empowerment of the syllable HŪṂ, wild beasts such as tigers and wolves, and malevolent humans and non-humans, are utterly unable to overcome or subdue him.
Thus it was when the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree.
By means of this mudrā and mantra, the hosts of celestial Māras are destroyed.
Since these three syllables possess such wondrous efficacy, they are recited repeatedly within the text. Next, ring the bell and chant:
The Dharani of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination clearly demonstrates that all phenomena mentioned above exist solely through causes and conditions, and that their very essence is empty.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "There has never been a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes and conditions;
therefore, there is no phenomenon that is not empty. Thus, the revolving wheel of the triple world belongs entirely to dependent origination. To realize this—
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) must rely on the power of divine mantras to transform birth and death into the cessation of suffering (*nirodha*).

After reciting the mantra, one attains mastery over the mind and mastery over phenomena; whatever one desires is not obstructed. What are the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*)?

They are called "causes" (*hetu*) because they revolve and induce the ripening of fruits, and "conditions" (*pratyaya*) because they mutually depend upon one another. This is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
What is called "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so on, up to "birth conditions aging and death," refers to this. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the absence of the clarity of wisdom.
Its essence is characterized by following along with delusion and darkness; it is the failure of *tathatā* (suchness) to maintain its own nature.
Through a single moment of false movement, there arises non-awakening (*abodha*), which obscures and covers the true nature. Therefore, it is called ignorance.
This refers to "delusion. Regarding "formations" (*saṃskāra*): the wholesome and unwholesome karma created during past times is termed "formations.

Because karma is produced by delusion, it is said that "ignorance conditions formations. Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it carries the meaning of "discernment. This is precisely the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Due to the cause of karma, it draws one into rebirth within the three realms, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) moves in delusion.

Having entered and entrusted itself to the mother’s womb, it is therefore said that "volitional formations condition consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyaya-vijñāna*). Once the embryo has been entrusted to the womb, there are the three factors of vitality (*āyu*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
After seven days, these undergo a transformation to become name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "Name" refers to the mind, and "form" refers to the physical substance;

thus it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form. Within this womb, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are formed. Since both mind and form are present, the six sense bases are thereby accomplished; thus it is said:
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Because the sense organs possess the function of entering into contact with their objects, they are called "bases.

As for contact (*sparśa*): after emerging from the womb, because the sense organs encounter their objects but have not yet attained discrimination, it is said that the six sense bases condition contact.
Feeling (*vedanā*) has the sense of experiencing; it experiences worldly phenomena such as the wholesome and the unwholesome, arising from the six sense organs contacting their respective objects.

Therefore, one subsequently experiences [feeling]. Thus it is said: "Contact is the condition for feeling. "Craving" refers to the longing for and delighting in worldly objects that are agreeable to the mind.

Because of the experience of feeling, craving subsequently arises. Thus it is said: "Feeling is the condition for craving. "Grasping" refers to the intention of seizing upon and clinging to without relinquishing.
One gives rise to grasping toward all objects; because grasping arises from craving, it is said: "Craving is the condition for grasping."

Grasping (*upādāna*). Because of attachment through grasping, one gives rise to afflictions and creates karma, which will lead to birth within the three realms of existence; therefore, it is said that "grasping conditions existence" (*upādānapratyayo bhavaḥ*).
Since the causes for the three realms of existence already exist, birth must necessarily occur; therefore, it is said that "existence conditions birth" (*bhavapratyayā jātiḥ*).

Since birth exists, there must necessarily be the fruits such as old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); these twelve links of dependent origination collectively encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time, like a spinning wheel.
The wheel of fire turns without rest. Ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the two causal links of the past.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are the five resultant links of the present. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are the three causal links of the present.

Birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the two resultant links of the future. These are collectively termed the "gate of forward progression" (*pravṛtti-mukha*). Now, since the practitioner...
Since beginningless kalpas, due to conditions such as ignorance (*avidyā*), one has experienced the bitter fruits of the present.

Now, by the power of the skillful means of observing through precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and through the merit of the protection of divine mantras, one illuminates that the essence and characteristics of the bodies and minds of oneself and others, as well as their objects, are all empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
There is nothing existent internally or externally; thus, this mind of mine is identical to the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.

This is called the gate of cessation (*nirodha-mukha*). Thus, the *Daśavidyā-śāstra* states: "To be deluded regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) is to be in the ocean of suffering;
this is termed a 'sentient being' (*sattva*). To realize that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the twelve links of existence is fundamentally empty is the Great Jewel Adorned City;
this is named a 'Buddha'. Now, through the power of the practitioner’s mantra, wisdom, and the merit of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), [this is realized].
This immediately causes the twelve links of dependent origination to become the ocean of the Buddha’s *pāramitās*.

As discussed above, by borrowing the provisional to manifest the real, subsuming phenomena into principle, and reconciling the conventional with emptiness, one cultivates the foundation of the myriad virtues.
"From me and the dharmadhātu, up to the Guru and the Three Jewels"—this begins the section clearly explaining how practice and aspiration support one another.
It describes constructing the maṇḍala, arranging offerings, adorning the pure land, and reaching out toward the holy ones. This refers to making aspirations before actually performing the practices.
In short, aspiration is the essential core of one's resolve. If one does not first strengthen the mind through firm aspiration, there is a fear that indolence will arise;
therefore, it is necessary to first generate the aspiration and take refuge in the Three Jewels. If one does not take refuge, whatever one undertakes will entirely become the activity of Māra.
Furthermore, by relying upon the secret influence and empowerment of the Guru and the Three Jewels, may my original aspiration be swiftly realized.
This is the accomplishment. The practitioner holds flowers and rice in their hands and says:
"I and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm. This clearly demonstrates that he does not generate this vast mind solely for himself.
From now until the time of realization, this clearly demonstrates the firmness of his vow and his constant lack of retreat or cowardice.
The vow to take refuge in the Guru and the Three Jewels clearly demonstrates that one’s resolve is vast, supreme, and unsurpassed.
The Vajra Guru occupies the foremost position among the Three Jewels because he is the Dharma upon which the Buddhas themselves rely. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"All Buddhas take the true nature (*dharmatā*) as their basis for all phenomena; relying upon this true nature, they generate the resolve and engage in cultivation."
One practices until Bodhi is finally attained. If one does not take this as one's teacher, all such beings are the Māra Pāpīyān. The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:
"The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher. The *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "When I first attained the Way, I contemplated who was worthy of reverence and praise."
There is nothing superior to the Dharma, for it is able to bring all ordinary beings and sages to liberation. Therefore, the Master is the Dharma itself.
"Vajra" is a metaphor for the true nature (*dharmatā*); it takes the meaning of being firm, sharp, and unchanging.
Thus, Mañjuśrī in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says that the land from which he comes is called the Golden World, and the Buddha who is his teacher is called [Akṣobhya].
The Tathāgata Moving Wisdom and others [reside in] the Golden World, which is a metaphor for the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Immovable Wisdom is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); this refers to the fact that the Vajra Master occupies the foremost position. This is what is meant.
*Namo guru-saṅghāya*. These four lines constitute the refuge in the Three Jewels: the first line is the refuge in the Guru;
the subsequent three lines are the refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Oṃ lili hahaca: this is the true Guru. Oṃ śrī mahāca: this is the true Triple Gem. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ.
Furthermore, recite these three syllables of the dhāraṇī to empower [the substances]. Sprinkle flowers and rice into the sky.
Emptiness. One visualizes the scattered precious rice as clouds of various offerings, such as flowers and incense, which are presented so that they become inexhaustible.
Next, invite the three presiding masters. First, extend a verse and burn incense to praise and invoke them, and then present the offerings.
Arranging incense and flowers (up to) upon a single hair-tip: spreading out famous incenses and fresh flowers like stars in the sky, one constructs this sublime altar of myriad jewels.
Within these infinitely layered and inexhaustible Buddha-realms, all are manifested within the characters upon my single hair-tip.

They do not obstruct one another. Yet, while the tip of a hair is not large and the Buddha-realm is not small, they are able to encompass all things universally and interpenetrate without mutual obstruction.
It is like a single cubit’s space manifesting a thousand layers of reflections.

This is the realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*), the gate of sovereign mastery where breadth and narrowness are without hindrance. As the Sūtra says: "Within the tip of a single hair, [all things] are manifested."
In the realm of the Jewel King, one sits within a single mote of dust and turns the Great Dharma Wheel; one enters at will into the Indra-net of mirrors and pearls.

The primary and secondary, the large and the small, mutually reflect through concealment and manifestation. This is not something achievable through clever intellect; it is simply because such is the natural response of the Dharma.
"The mind merges with the wondrous principle" (up to) "the Dharma-realm is vast. These two lines praise the virtue of the Dharmakāya.

This means that when the mind and the wondrous principle are in perfect union, one immediately perceives the Dharmakāya as expansive and boundless; looking back at the mundane world, empty space appears like a single drop in the ocean.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "At that time, Ānanda received the subtle and wonderful instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata..."

Body and mind become utterly serene, attaining non-obstruction. Each member of this great assembly perceives their own mind pervading the ten directions and sees the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in the palm of one's hand; such is the meaning of this. "The Way" refers to the practice of wisdom.
It means that if this practice of wisdom accords with and perfectly merges with True Suchness (Tathatā), then one perceives the Dharma-realm.

This nature extends vertically through the three periods of time and spans horizontally throughout the ten directions; it is vast and boundless, like a person entering the ocean who perceives ever greater depth and breadth.
This is the meaning of the *dharmadhātu* of principle.
"Physical marks and signs, compassion, and kindness (up to) 'dense evening clouds. This praises the wisdom-virtue of the *saṃbhogakāya*. Now, as for the Buddha’s fundamental body (*mūlakāya*):
this body possesses immeasurable colors; these colors possess immeasurable marks; and these marks possess immeasurable signs.

Compassion, joy, equanimity, and so forth are all fully perfected, just like the full moon in autumn, complete and without flaw. This praises the two [bodies], the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*."
Regarding the virtue of liberation of the body: it is said that the Buddha’s transformation bodies traverse the ten directions, responding to the capacities of beings within the six realms.
They are as solemn as evening clouds; they arise in profusion and leap forth with vigor, surging spontaneously and boundlessly, vast and dense beyond anyone’s grasp.
These two constitute the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Within this mass of incense smoke, the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the Buddha are contained within the Ocean Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). Their divine mystery is unfathomable; all who seek receive response, and there is no wish that is not fulfilled.

Tranquil and unmoving, they respond and thereby bring about universal penetration. Now, within this mass of incense smoke, I— [...]* (The text continues with the practitioner’s visualization and invocation). *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the liturgical text.*

One gazes toward the manifested form-body (rūpakāya) as it descends, appearing with distinct clarity like the myriad images contained within the ocean, or like characters formed by a seal, without requiring any sequence of before or after. As the ancient masters said: "The clear pool is limpid and pure;
the bright mirror hangs empty. The myriad phenomena are arrayed therein, reflected in vast, open void. Now, with sincere faith and a single thought of profound stillness, [the Buddha appears].
Thus, the thousand sages find their constant refuge and the myriad spirits congregate; how could this pertain solely to the presiding masters of the three altars?
These two points constitute the meaning of the unimpeded dharma-realm of principle and phenomena, and they form the text for the formal invocation.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata is the teacher of the Sahā world and the fourth Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa.

In the Sanskrit language, "Śākya" means "Capable One" (Nengren); this signifies one who possesses benevolence and compassion to provide succor to sentient beings. "Muni" in Sanskrit means "Silent One" (Jimo);
it refers to one who has eternally stilled the two extremes and attained silent realization of the Middle Way. "Tathāgata" means "One who has come from Thusness."
Therefore, he is named Tathāgata; this is the name by which Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed his prediction upon him. I now request him to bear witness and grant his seal of approval:
as I now perform the ritual according to the teachings, the Buddha will surely grant his sanction.

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—this is explained as before—is the teacher of the nectar of immortality (amṛta). We pray that you will secretly bestow your protective grace, so that all our undertakings may be accomplished.
Venerable Ānanda was the master who established expedient means and inaugurated the teaching; he was the patriarch of the ritual for bestowing food.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Ānanda, which here is translated as "Joyous Celebration. He was the younger cousin of the Tathāgata and was foremost among those of great learning.

For it is because the Dharma does not arise in isolation, but is born only by relying upon conditions, that he first employed expedient transformations to benefit future generations. Thus, he practiced in the midst of the groves.
While in meditative concentration, he beheld a formless apparition at night. He returned to seek refuge with the Buddha, piteously pleading for a means to alleviate his suffering.
The Buddha manifested the divine verses of majestic virtue and fully opened the Dharma-gate of the Ambrosia. Thereupon, the dark path was suddenly illuminated and all things were restored to spring.
Had it not been for the compassionate mind of the Venerable One manifesting through skillful means, how could there have been this teaching on the offering of food?
Ring the bell and recite the verse on self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*) and "self-nature": "Expedient" (*fang*) refers to the Dharma; "means" (*bian*) refers to what is appropriate.
This means that by employing skillful methods, one accords with the capacities and needs of sentient beings, such as manifesting bodies that are not fixed. By means of this wondrous essence...

Originally free from all characteristics, it manifests various characteristics for the sake of all sentient beings; yet all such characteristics are merely provisional means (*upāya*) that follow conditions for a single period.
The essence of this nature of skillful means is like gold that does not change, or like steel that is firm and sharp;
even when mixed with dust and ore, its substance is not destroyed, and when cast into a great furnace, its color does not alter. It is not affected by external things.

That which is destroyed and that which destroys all things—by means of this essential nature, though it is unchanging, it can adapt to conditions (*pratyaya*) and manifest birth within the three realms to share in the sufferings of the people.
Furthermore, it can sever the net of ignorance (*moha*) of sentient beings and shatter the fortress-city of afflictions (*kleśa*);
therefore, it is likened to a diamond (*vajra*), which is fundamentally indestructible. The Great Hero is able to...

He is the conqueror of enemies and the one who can terrify the armies of Māra. The "Great Knower" refers to the Omniscient One, whose wisdom illumines all things without exception throughout both the mundane and supramundane realms;
it is said that only the Buddha is capable of such knowledge.

It is supremely peerless (up to: "all are accomplished"). Although it is unchanging, it does not obstruct following conditions; although it follows conditions, it does not obstruct its unchanging nature.
For this reason, it is most extremely sublime and beyond comparison. It skillfully transcends all realms of existence and surpasses all worldly burdens.
Its numinous awareness is absolute and without dependence, standing far beyond the reach of thought and deliberation. Therefore, it is called "transcendent."
[The] marks. Since the Buddha’s original nature was thus, I now vow that what I practice shall likewise achieve this wondrous body.
The four lines above praise the substance of the Buddha’s manifested body; the four lines below properly praise the substance of the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
From the nature of supreme wisdom up to the sound of the wheel of Dharma: the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
its gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Even if śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
It is also that which cannot be known; therefore, it is called "supreme wisdom" (*jñāna*). Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is most profoundly deep.
Because it is so profound, one is able to manifest the sound of the Dharma. Why is the Dharma called a "wheel" (*cakra*)? A wheel has the meaning of "pushing and turning.
By turning this Wheel of the Dharma, one is able to shatter the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings and transform the ordinary into the holy.
The Sūtra states: "From fundamental wisdom flows subsequently attained wisdom; from subsequently attained wisdom flows the mind of great compassion;
and from the mind of great compassion flow the twelve divisions of the teaching. Therefore, all expounded teachings take wisdom as their essential nature.
By means of non-arising, [the manifestation] up to the fulfillment of vows is accomplished. In preaching the Dharma, he does not depart from his body;

yet that body is fundamentally bodiless—it is merely manifested through skillful means as various bodies. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "At that time, I appeared in the world and employed skillful means for the sake of sentient beings."
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is such that they manifest through skillful means a body of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Since they have done so, I too should do likewise; thus it is said: "May this vow now performed be fulfilled.
The wisdom of the Buddha-body is thus profoundly deep and subtle, supreme and peerless. Yet, while there has never been an untainted (*anāsrava*) body, one relies upon a tainted (*sāsrava*)...
Therefore, one recites the verses for purifying the ground to transform impurity into purity, so that the various sages and worthies may dwell in peace and security.
"In all directions" (up to) "none exist at all" refers to the layout of the maṇḍala to be established hereafter;
it is not like the Sahā world, which is filled with filth and impurities, such as earth, stones, mountains, tiles, rubble, sand, gravel, pits, and hollows.
Mounds and hills—places that were uneven and impure—have now all been transformed into a ground of lapis lazuli jewels.
Regarding this "ground of lapis lazuli jewels" (up to) the phrase "may [all] vows be fulfilled": beneath the ocean floor there is a stone that is most perfectly level and full;
being as flat as the palm of a hand and as soft as cotton, it is subtle and wondrous beyond compare. We pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will abide here.

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the ground is composed of exquisite jewels; the gardens are made of various precious gems. There are jade groves and crystalline trees, with lofty towers stretching afar;
there are golden terraces and silver trees, with galleries extending alongside. The roof-beams and structures support one another, while windows and doors reflect each other’s light.
The steps, courtyards, railings, and balustrades, as well as the ponds, pools, and flower forests—all such things are perfectly complete, all fashioned from exquisite jewels. This is the Dharma...
Wherever the sound is proclaimed, there is nothing that is not fully perfected.
From the supramundane [state]... until "may you abide in peace. While the Tathāgata was in the world, he transformed this Sahā world into a pure land;
now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, none are able to manifest it again. I, following the Dharma of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, am now once more able to...
May this ground, composed of various kinds of the seven precious jewels, with immeasurable radiance illuminating both the interior and exterior,
resplendent and magnificent— wherever its light shines— be the place where all the sages and holy ones dwell, remaining steadfast and unmoving.

At this point, one should present offerings. Recite the mantra for washing the feet (*pādaprakṣālana-mantra*), form the lotus mudrā (*padma-mudrā*), recite the five Brahma-offerings (*pañca-brahmāñjali*), distribute the *dakṣiṇā*, and recite the *sīmāla* mantra. Thus, there exists the mantra for washing and bathing the feet, which signifies the intent of cleansing the feet.
As the *Book of Songs* says: "The waters of Canglang are clear; with them I may wash my cap-strings. The waters of Canglang are turbid..."
...whereby one may wash one's feet. One chants the *Music Mantra* (Yinyue Zhou) and places bells upon the table. One recites the *Pure Ground Mantra* (Jingdi Zhou) and the *Music Mantra*.
Whenever these mantras are chanted, it is as if the celestial music of the Jade Emperor were being performed everywhere:

the five notes are harmonious and elegant, the six pitch-pipes flow together in resonance, and their subtle and wondrous power penetrates all, making offerings to the Triple Gem of the ten directions.
Oṃ vajramahāmaya hūṃ. First, this generally explains the arising of the causes of the world. As a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"In the realm of space, a great wind arises, its lateral breadth immeasurable and its thickness twelve lakṣas;
it cannot be destroyed even by a diamond. This is called the 'Wind that Sustains the Realm. From the clouds of the Ābhāsvara Heaven and the Golden Treasury, rain falls throughout the trichiliocosm."

the essence of illumination stands alone, and the spirit has no fixed location. What need, then, would there be for a land? Nevertheless, there still manifest the distinctions between the defiled and the pure.

This means that there is nothing that is not established as a transformation to guide and lead various capacities at the proper time. Having completed the explanation of the causes for the initial establishment of the mandala,

To the east of the lake flows the Gaṅgā River, emerging from the mouth of an elephant; together with five hundred other rivers, it flows into the eastern ocean.
In the ocean, to the south of the lake, is the Sindhu River; it issues from the Ox’s Mouth and flows into the Southern Ocean together with five hundred rivers.
To the west of the lake is the Vakṣu River; it issues from the Horse’s Mouth and flows into the Western Ocean together with five hundred rivers.

Manifestation. Therefore, when performing rituals below [this level], there are many instances where one transforms the physical form and color;

There is no demonic obstruction. Furthermore, the mental activities of those Māras and their like most delight in creating the causes and conditions for the destruction of the Dharma.

there was none who was not struck with wonder and alarm. These ordinary beings, shrouded in darkness, do not perceive the shifting calamities.

They have all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); yet they remain attached to these worldly toils—how could they ever allow you to destroy them?

They tear open that place; therefore, at the time of samādhi, they all come to disturb and disrupt meditative concentration, preventing your True Dharma from reaching fulfillment and ensuring that their own māra-palaces remain secure and free from peril.

Consequently, when a practitioner performs ritual practices now, one fears the presence of various obstacles caused by the *viṣaya-māras* (obstacles of sensory realms), as well as the celestial *māras*, the *skandha-māras* (aggregates), and other such diverse *māras*.
Because they are obstructive, they must be expelled.
The mantra for expelling māras, the triple mantra, and the triple expulsion of māras: first, the expulsion of māras.
From the red syllable *hūṃ* atop the mudrā, light radiates forth, expelling the māras of objective spheres—that is, the māras of favorable and unfavorable objects. Next, the expulsion of māras:

from the seal, ten times the red syllable *HŪṂ* emits vajra-flames that fan the sky, causing the māras to depart. Vajra.
Regarding "flame" (*jvālā*): Yongjia said, "The sharpness of Prajñā is like adamantine flame;
it not only emptily crushes the minds of externalists, but has long since lost the courage of the heavenly Māras. This is a statement made from the perspective of principle (*li*).
If considered from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), it refers to the fire-wheel, the *vajra*, Ucchuṣma, and the *tejo-jvālā-samādhi*. These superior powers of wisdom all accord with [the truth].

The commentary explains this: if one relies on the manifestation of phenomena (*dharmas*), the meaning becomes even more profound. For instance, when first ascending the altar, one might rely on the conceit that "I am the Dharma-King" and possess mastery over all phenomena, establishing them wherever one goes.
Now, fearing that one may become deluded regarding oneself and pursue external objects, failing to realize that they are like illusions, it is necessary to dispel such notions.
Regarding the various phenomena thus established, if one does not know that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is fundamentally empty, one will cling to them.

To regard [phenomena] as truly existent is called the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Furthermore, to falsely conceptualize within phenomena that there is a truly existent sovereign is called the attachment to self (*ātman-grāha*).
From these two attachments, the two obstacles arise. Above, one is unable to transform the basis for the two fruits;
below, how does this differ from the views of Māras and non-Buddhists? In the Sanskrit language, *māra*; here it is translated as "the slayer," for they are able to injure and destroy the Dharma.
Because one’s body is the life-force of wisdom and because one treasures the virtues of the kalpas, the first seal signifies the elimination of the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*).

This is because it is coarse and thus easy to sever. The second seal signifies the elimination of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This is because it is subtle and thus difficult to remove.

Once these two graspings are eliminated, one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, which is called "universal emptiness" (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*). If one dwells in this emptiness, it is termed an "obstruction to principle. Therefore...
Emptiness is also empty; this is called the "severing of both emptinesses" and corresponds to the third seal.

Because that which cannot be emptied is precisely the fundamental source of true emptiness and non-abiding, the origin of all ordinary beings and sages, it is subsequently stabilized by the Seal of True Emptiness.
The mantra and mudrā of the true void (continue until) there is no interruption. When reciting the mantra, one should visualize a golden syllable *Oṃ* upon the moon disc of the heart.
This is called the Great Wisdom Great Wheel Vajra Samādhi that Adorns All Buddha-fields.
Having entered this meditative absorption, one is able to establish all phenomena from the groundless root. *Dharmapada-sūtra*.
It is said: Within ultimate emptiness, the Bodhisattva vigorously establishes all phenomena;
thus, within the self-nature of true emptiness, they silently contemplate *Pūṃ Phaṭ ĀḤ HŪṂ*. In a single thought-moment, the entire world-system of the ten directions is instantaneously perfected.
All the wondrous celestial maṇḍalas and the five offerings of *arya-gan* are like the clouds of Samantabhadra gathering to present offerings.
This clearly explains that the mind of making offerings is vast. "Pervading space and filling the realms" clarifies that these offerings extend horizontally throughout the ten directions.
"Exhausting saṃsāra without interval" reveals that these offerings reach vertically through the three periods of time. Question:
How can these three syllables accomplish such a supreme feat? The answer is: the syllables *Aṃ* and *Hrīḥ*.
As previously stated regarding "adorned with all [excellences]," and as the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"This mantra can destroy the sufferings of all hell realms, the realm of Yama, and the animal kingdom; it causes beings to turn toward the good paths, and even to the pure lands of the Buddhas."
As well as the palaces of the various devas and all the profound spheres of practice of the bodhisattvas, they enter them at will without any obstruction.

Upon relinquishing their retribution, they are immediately reborn in buddha-fields and so forth. The syllable *A* is named the entry into the non-differentiated realm through the majestic power of the bodhisattvas;
it also signifies the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). The syllable *Hūṃ* is named the bodhi of all Tathāgatas.
The mind is the cause. It is also said that the ocean-like merits of all Tathāgatas arise from this very source. To speak of it in general terms:

taking the bodhicitta as the cause, one enters the profound sphere of practice of the Bodhisattvas, adorning all Buddha-fields and the sublime maṇḍalas of the celestial palaces; ultimately, all these converge in a single reality.

This is the realm of non-differentiation of characteristics. Question: Since all the various jewels of the four continents are already fully and perfectly accomplished above, what is the significance of constructing them again here?
Answer: All that has been performed above belongs to the gradual stage and cannot be complete in its entirety.
Here, everything is accomplished simultaneously through the power of the mantra; otherwise, one might fear losing the essential principle of "mind-only."

Furthermore, there are three types of dispatching [the visualization]. Fearing that one might fall into a state of mere emptiness and quiescence, one should, within a single thought-moment, contemplate the power of these three syllables from within the self-nature of true emptiness;
they will then manifest instantaneously in a kṣaṇa, perfected in a single thought. Therefore, the subsequent verse states:
"Each syllable is a secret mantra, accomplished solely by the mind. Thus, we know that the former belongs to the gradual process, while this refers to instantaneous perfection in a single thought.

Therefore, there is no confusion. The above establishment of all phenomena (dharmas) is entirely dependent upon causes and conditions. The flower and rice serve as the cause, while the mantra serves as the condition;
furthermore, they are accomplished through the single thought-moment of "mind-only. It is by relying on these causes and conditions that all established phenomena subsequently come into being.
Since all phenomena belong to the realm of causes and conditions, their very essence is emptiness. Although they are empty...

It does not hinder the manifestation of existence; yet existence is eternally empty of itself. Even if existence were to appear, its very substance is emptiness; emptiness eternally penetrates existence.

This non-obstruction between emptiness and existence is the contemplation of the Middle Way. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty;
they are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. This is precisely what that refers to.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. With the scattering of flowers and grains, one forms offerings such as precious jewels.

Furthermore, one presents these through three invocations of the maṇḍala according to both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions, while praying that the Buddhas accept them and requesting the fulfillment of one's aspirations.
Contemplate with clarity and purity... [until] compassionately accept [this]. *Suvarṇa* in the Sanskrit language means "gold. *Rūpya* in the Sanskrit language means "white silver.
As for "precious gems," these belong to the class of various jewels. *Masāragalva* in the Sanskrit language means "lapis lazuli";
it is also called "water-jade" (*shuiyu*), which refers to crystal. *Vaidūrya* in the Sanskrit language means... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The blue jewel is transparent both inside and out. In Sanskrit it is called *pāramagha*, which here is translated as "red pearl" (*zhū*) or "coral.
Amber is not the red pearl; rather, this refers to the celestial red pearl. Its crimson light radiates in all directions, and its jewel-like colors intermingle in a brilliant splendor.
It is also called Indra-ratna (Indra-jewel), which does not exist in the mundane world. In the Sanskrit language it is *pāṣmāragaḷa*, which here is translated as agate;
it is also called "stone-heart. *Śaṅkha* is also known as the "great conch pearl. As for "precious jewel," it refers to the *maṇi* pearl.
"I now rely upon the teachings [until] there is no interruption. This is the second offering. These three verses are most clearly expressed;
there is no need for a detailed commentary. Place the bell on the table. Next, holding flowers and rice with the right hand, recite as follows:
I pray only that the Guru and the Triple Gem... Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ. Having thus made the great aspiration, take refuge in the Triple Gem and request their witness.
Then recite the three-syllable *dhāraṇī* mantra while scattering flowers and rice.

Visualize that the scattered precious rice and grains all become clouds of fragrant flowers and so forth, which are offered as worship. Those above are the Triple Gem of the same essence; those below—
This praises the distinct characteristics of the Triple Gem and so forth, giving rise to the hearts of longing and admiration among sentient beings, thereby fulfilling the seed of Buddhahood.
"With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage" (up to) "endowed with myriad virtues. "With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage" is a term denoting refined reverence.

In the Sanskrit language, *buddha*; here it is translated as "Awakened. An Awakened One refers to one who has reached the ultimate end of the five abodes [of ignorance] and forever forgotten the two deaths. As...
Awakening from the great dream, the lotus flower blooms; thus he is named Buddha. With merit fulfilled and wisdom fulfilled, he is named the Honored One Among the Two-Legged.

Having awakened himself and awakened others, with the perfection of awakening and practice, he is named the One Perfect in the Three Awakenings. He is fully endowed with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

He is named "Endowed with Myriad Virtues. Because his cause was perfected, his fruition was manifested; he guides and instructs humans and devas, thus being called the "Tamer and Controller" (*śāstṛ*).

"Taming" means to subdue; "controlling" means to skillfully drive [the vehicle] according to the occasion. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are by nature stubborn and violent."
Difficult to discipline and difficult to subdue, only the Tathāgata employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), employing various words of urgent exhortation to transform them.
This is because the minds of those who are difficult to transform are like monkeys;
therefore, by restraining their minds through various kinds of dharmas, they can finally be disciplined and enter the Vinaya. For this reason, he is named "Buddha."
"Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, the Teacher who Tames Gods and Humans. These are none other than empowered sounds that bring about vast praise.

As stated in the *Pranidhāna-paṭala*: "In all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, as numerous as atoms, and within each atom, there are Buddhas as numerous as those very atoms;
I shall perceive them all before me with profound faith and understanding."
Each, by means of the subtle tongue-roots of the goddess Sarasvatī that transcend all, produces from each individual tongue-root an inexhaustible ocean of sounds;

from each ocean of sounds, they produce an ocean of all speech and words, extolling and praising the oceans of virtues of all Tathāgatas, continuing without interruption throughout the entirety of the future. This is the intended meaning.

He is the Great Compassionate Father of all ordinary beings and sages, the refuge for the three classes of sages and the six realms of existence; thus he is called the "Compassionate Father. As a sutra states:
"Having perfected the five eyes and attained Bodhi, he shall forever act as the Compassionate Father for the triple world."
From the True Realm (up to) the locations of the ten directions. The following praises the manifestation of the body and the preaching of the Dharma:

that is to say, the Tathāgata emerges from the single True Dharma-realm as a responsive and transformative substance, like the bright moon in the empty sky appearing simultaneously in a thousand rivers.
The compassionate mind of transformation is omnipresent. Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time; horizontally, it encompasses and pervades the ten directions.
To "thunder the Dharma-thunder" carries the sense of providing awakening.
Beating the Dharma drum carries the significance of advancing one’s resolve.
It extensively expounds the provisional and the real teachings: the Three Vehicles are the provisional, while the One Vehicle is the real.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ—greatly opening the path of skillful means. As the Sūtra says: "All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally and naturally quiescent and extinguished."

The marks cannot be proclaimed in words. Now, the Buddha manifests his body within the bodiless and preaches the Dharma within the non-Dharmas, skillfully conforming to the capacities of beings and establishing teachings according to the times; this is why it is called the opening of expedient means.
Regarding the passage from "If one takes refuge... up to "...the suffering of hell," the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith) states: "To awaken is to be unmoving; to move is to have suffering.
The fruit does not depart from the cause, for the fruit is produced by the cause. Because of a single moment of non-awakening, the mind moves; this is termed "karma" (*karman*).

Since the cause of karma exists, how could the fruit of suffering not exist? If one can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back within, one immediately returns to what was originally attained, and thus rides upon [the vehicle].
By the power of this Prajñā, what suffering of the hells could one fear that would not be avoided?

With a sincere heart, one should believe and pay homage... [until] it was transmitted to the Eastern Land. Ānanda compiled the various sūtras in the Piṭhara Cave in the Western Regions. Thus it is said:
"The waters of the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flow into the heart of Ānanda. Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:

They protect and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. Next, there were the Tripiṭaka Masters and others who translated and transmitted [the teachings] to the Eastern Lands, rendering the Sanskrit language into the Chinese language; this is called "translation."

The Patriarchs propagated [the Dharma] without being entangled with either ordinary beings or sages; they were transcendent, and thus they were called "Patriarchs" (*zu*). To "propagate" (*hong*) means to widely open and disseminate [the teaching].

The worthy and wise judged that although they practiced according to the teachings, they had not yet fully penetrated the source of the mind; they were merely approaching the state of a sage. Therefore...
This is what is meant by being called "worthy and wise. As for "discernment," it refers to discerning and classifying the various teachings into the "Half" and the "Full.
Teachings of definitive meaning are called "Full," while those of non-definitive meaning are called "Half-letters."
The Preface to the Commentary (up to the section on "Determining the Essential Tenet"): Explaining the principles and meanings, the commentary was composed instantaneously.
Regarding the "Three Vehicles": these are the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas. "Sudden" means that it reveals only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision without establishing gradual stages;

by merely departing from deluded conditions, one is immediately like the Buddha. "Gradual" means extensively clarifying the stages of practice and cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, each standing distinctively [from the other].

Regarding "nature and characteristics" (*xingxiang*): it is the resolution of the true and the false. Regarding the "five teachings": they are the Small, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect. That which is revered by a particular division is called its "tenet" (*zong*);
that toward which the tenet leads is called its "destination" (*qu*).
The ghosts and spirits revere [it], up to the point of the True Nectar. A sutra states: "The teaching of the Sūtras is like a finger pointing at the moon;
it causes people to rely on the finger to recognize the moon. Once the moon is seen, one forgets the finger; by all means, do not mistake the finger for the moon. Therefore, it is called a "pointer."

If one takes refuge [up to] from the suffering of hungry ghosts: the karmic causes for being a hungry ghost are mostly stinginess, greed, and refusal to relinquish, coupled with an empty stomach and a haughty mind.
Due to these karmic causes, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts; yet now, by taking refuge, one tears down the banner of pride.
Now that you have heard and understood this, you will realize the emptiness of all phenomena; how could you again look back upon the fruit of empty flowers or erect the mountain of the great self?
Furthermore, why worry about the suffering of hungry ghosts that you cannot escape?
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage... (up to) "this household duty. *Saṃgha* means "harmonious assembly" (*ho-ho-jung*).

Just as various streams flow into the ocean and share the same salty taste, so too do those of various surnames who have left the home life share the same surname, Gautama; they are called "harmonious" because they are like water and milk blending together.

They are called "the Honored One among the Assembly" because their wisdom is lofty, their talent is vast, their conduct is upright, and their virtue is eminent, such that they are revered and looked up to by all. Five.

Regarding virtue (*guṇa*): first, one’s speech is single-minded and not coarse or harsh; second, one expounds the Dharma to benefit others without weariness; third, one’s purity of precepts and virtue is widely renowned;
fourth, one is able to eliminate the poisonous harms of afflictions (*kleśa*); fifth, one constantly dwells together with the Buddhas. Regarding harmony (*sāmagrī*): [the following six points apply].

They dwell in harmony of body; they are harmonious in speech and free from contention; they are harmonious in mind and share mutual joy; they are harmonious in view and share the same understanding; they are harmonious in precepts and practice them together;

they are harmonious in material goods and distribute them equally. Taking the welfare of sentient beings as their occupation and the propagation of the Dharma as their task, they do not shrink from sacrificing their bodies or losing their lives.

This clearly demonstrates that propagating the Dharma for the sake of the Sangha is not a matter beyond one's proper sphere. The former praises the eminent monks who enter the marketplace and extend their hands in grace;
the latter clarifies the venerable elders who practice the ascetic dhūta austerities.
Avoiding the clamor and dust [until] he gathered mugwort for firewood. Weary of the heat, he rejoiced in stillness;

he withdrew in secret from the mundane world to sit in meditative repose amidst secluded mountains and forests. He took up residence beneath crags and in stone chambers. Though revered by humans and devas, he felt no joy.
He gathered mugwort for firewood to fill his belly and donned coarse woolen robes to cover his body, using clumps of grass as a cushion.
"Bending the arm to use it as a pillow" is to find joy in the Way.
Regarding the "Bowl that Subdued the Dragon," it was transmitted and entrusted [to the patriarchs]. Maudgalyāyana, the Sixth Patriarch, and others used the bowl to subdue dragons.

When Deng Yinfeng heard two tigers fighting, he flew his *zhishi* (monk’s staff) through the air, making a sound that caused them to disperse. [This refers to] the Forty-Eight [Patriarchs] of the Western Heaven and the [patriarchs] of the East...

From the second and third patriarchs of the soil [China] up to the five schools and their various lineages, the great masters of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya have either transmitted the Dharma through the Dharma or sealed mind with mind.
It is like one lamp transmitting its light to another; as lamp after lamp continues in succession, their brilliance remains inexhaustible.
It is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp," which illuminates the world to its furthest reaches without ceasing; hence it is said that "the Dharma-lamp constantly shines everywhere.
As for "transmitting the ancestral seal," this refers to the successive transmission and entrustment of the mind-seal of the patriarchs.
If one takes refuge [up to] the suffering of animals (*tiryagyoni*). "Animals" refers to those born among the domesticated beasts and wild creatures.
Since the Jewel of the Sangha is the path to liberation, once one falls into the animal realm, one is subjected to various afflictions:
being confined in cages by humans, being hunted with bows and crossbows, being caught in fishing nets, and being butchered and carved by cooks. Even if one is a bird or a beast, [one suffers].

They constantly harbor the sorrow of frantic wandering; strong and weak, large and small, devour one another in turn. They labor to repay their debts of strength, exchanging services for recompense, never attaining liberation.
Once they take refuge in the Sangha Jewel, wisdom suddenly awakens, and they tear asunder the net of ignorance.
With hearts turned toward one another through compassion, they lay down the hands that wield bows and arrows in combat. Possessing such supreme power, how [could they not be saved]?
Is one not to fear the suffering of the animal realm? At this point, one may accommodate the sentiments of the donor.
Furthermore, the practitioner should inspire the assembly to resolve upon Bodhicitta; next, they should take refuge in the Triple Gem and give rise to the supreme mind.
May the assembly give rise to the vast mind [up to] the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

As for the meritorious retributions of humans and devas, the causes and effects of the outflows within the triple world, and the solitary liberation of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, these seek only self-benefit and disregard their original kin.

The provisional vehicles refer to the *zàng* (Treasury) and *tōng* (Penetrating) teachings and the Mahāyāna *yuán* (Perfect) teaching, which involve the cultivation of the six *pāramitās* and so forth.
The Supreme Vehicle is the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). *Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*wu-shang*); *samyak* means "rightly equal" (*zheng-deng*); and *sambodhi*.

This is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). To speak truly, one should give rise to this great vow not merely for oneself, seeking the fruits of the human or celestial realms, the Lesser Vehicle, or even the Bodhisattva path, but rather vow that all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu* may simultaneously attain this path of unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Having thus resolved the mind, one then requests the Buddhas of the ten directions to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, so that...

Once all those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will then suddenly shatter their ignorance and develop their originally inherent enlightened nature, spontaneously attaining unsurpassed Bodhi.

When one wishes to widely welcome the various sages and greatly turn the Wheel of Dharma, one must first purify and prepare the ritual site, making it solemn and magnificent, before it is fit for the invitation. Therefore:
Next is the binding of the Vidyārāja mudrā.
First, bind the Great Wheel [mudrā] and recite the mantra seven times. As for following the instructions:

this refers to the ritual for the recitation of the Bodhisattva Amṛtakuṇḍalin, which teaches the holding of the secret words of the mantra to cause the vast palace that I have created to become supremely wondrous and adorned.
All shall be fully accomplished without any obstacles. Recite [the mantra] silently seven times.
One should visualize, in the space before oneself at a height of seven to eight cubits from the body, the appearance of a golden syllable *praṃ*.
This syllable is named the "Vajra Samādhi of the Great Wisdom Great Wheel that Adorns All Buddha-fields. Upon entering this samādhi, one is able to...
One should transform it into a supreme and wondrous palace. One should merge the great trichiliocosm into a single world-system, and with this world-system, form a single palace.
Each of its adornments and various ritual implements shall be as described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, wherein there are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers of supreme and wondrous delights.
Question: Regarding the aforementioned purification of the site and the construction of the maṇḍala...
[Question: "If each [deity] possesses its own altar, palace, and various ritual implements, how can there be any overlap? [Answer:
"What has been performed thus far is merely an establishment; it appears to have distinctions of 'this' and 'that,' and has not yet reached the state of universal equality."
If these were not brought together and fused into a single ground, it would be difficult to manifest the ultimate principle.

Therefore, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face; those lights shone brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns, causing the Buddha-worlds to tremble in six ways.
Thus, the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, were all revealed at once. The Buddha...
By the majestic spiritual power [of this mantra], all worlds are made to merge into a single realm. When deluded thoughts coalesce, the lands appear as distinct divisions;
when true wisdom arises, the Dharma-realm manifests perfectly. The present fusion of worlds is likewise so.
It is simply that by removing deluded thoughts, the lands remain as they are naturally; how much more so when relying on the power of divine mantras—what obstacle could possibly prevent it?
It is accomplished. First, defilement was overturned to reveal purity; next, the provisional was manifested from emptiness;

now, the world-realm is fused to become a palace, such that the dimensions of this palace equal those of the great trichiliocosm—vast and boundless, layered and inexhaustible, capable of accommodating infinite sages and worthies. Having thus adorned the palace, thereafter...
In order to invite the various holy ones, one first extends this verse of homage and invitation.
"I prostrate to the ten directions" [up to] "may you compassionately accept. Regarding "prostrate" (kai-shou): it means to bring the head to the ground and remain there for a short while.
The *dhāraṇī* can cause one’s three karmas to take refuge [in the Triple Gem]. When the mind gives rise to reverent acceptance, it evokes the Buddha’s supernormal power of knowing others’ minds;
when the body and head perform prostrations, it evokes the Buddha’s supernormal power of the divine eye; when the mouth recites the name, it evokes the Buddha’s supernormal power of the divine ear.

The Tamer of the Ten Directions is the Buddha-Gem. The proclamation of a single phrase is the Dharma-Gem. A single phrase of the Three Vehicles is the Sangha-Gem. Compassion is able to bestow [benefit].
The bliss of the *dharmatā*. Compassion (*karuṇā*) can extract the suffering of ignorance; "to receive with pity" is the formal invitation.
"I reverently invite the Triple Gem to grace this Dharma assembly"—this is the manifest invitation. Next, one performs the secret invitation through the light of the mind.
Having thus made these three earnest requests, how could the various sages not deign to attend? They shall now appear at the altar ritual being established.
And one makes offerings to it.
Regarding the manifestation of the mandala ritual through mudrās: although the mandala ritual is manifested, the intention also encompasses secret invocation.

This means that the maṇḍala established above appears simultaneously upon the mudrā, just as a seal produces its inscription; it is accomplished without depending on a sequence of before and after. This is the correct [method].
That which is called the myriad phenomena of the universe is the manifestation of a single Dharma-seal. As for making offerings to the Buddha, it is just as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:
"The various Brahmā devas each held their palaces and offered them to the Buddha," which shares the same intent as the exhortation to the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
According to the *Ritual for Constructing the Altar*, if there is no altar, there is no Buddha; one should...
The *Bodhisattva Dharmacakrapravartana-mudrā* is formed as soon as the intention arises.
Now, as one is about to invite the Buddha to preach the Dharma, this mudrā must first be formed to manifest the ritual of the maṇḍala. Next, invite the Buddha while reciting:
Oṃ vajra-cakra hūṃ ca hūṃ phaṭ. Form the Vajra-fist with both hands; interlock the fingers of wisdom and effort, facing each other at the chest. One should...
Visualize a white syllable *hrīḥ* upon the moon-disc of the mind radiating light. This light reaches the Akaniṣṭha Heaven to invite the Wisdom Avalokiteśvara.
This heaven is the place where Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment attain Buddhahood; their physical bodies are supremely vast and tall, measuring six hundred and forty thousand *yojanas*.
When the Bodhisattva enters the ritual arena, they emit immeasurable light and first invite the ten...

When the Three Jewels and the protective deities of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings had thus assembled, they emitted light from one another, their rays interlacing like a lattice of precious silk threads.
This brilliance was so magnificent and dazzling that it was a rare and auspicious sight. Question:

In all the teachings, the fruit is taken as the primary focus and the cause as its accompaniment. Now, when Avalokiteśvara emits light to summon and invite the Buddhas, why is this considered a "cause"?
Is he the primary fruit or the attendant? Answer: There are two meanings to this.
First, for the practitioner, Avalokiteśvara is the matured object of focus; by first attuning to this object, the cause encompasses the fruit.

Second, this Bodhisattva was formerly the Tathāgata Vīryaprabhāsvaravibhu who, having relinquished his sovereign position, descended to deliver sentient beings; although he manifests as the cause, he is fundamentally the fruit.
This is the station. Avalokiteśvara is fundamentally designated as "Compassion" (Pī); why is he now designated as "Wisdom" (Jñāna)? It is because without wisdom, one cannot mobilize compassion.
*Jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ* refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*): the hook, the noose, the chain, and the bell. "Hook" means to summon; "noose," to bind.
The "attracting" [mudrā], the "locking," the "retaining," and the "ring" which signifies "delight"—these are called the four *cakra-vartī* mudrās.
If discussed in terms of their symbolic meaning, they correspond to the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*): generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation. As the Sūtra says:
First one uses the hook of desire to lead them forward, and afterwards causes them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom. As in the case of the woman Vāsudhārā:
holding hands and embracing the body, the moon of the mind becomes pure; kissing the lips and savoring the tongue, the jewel of the precepts becomes perfect.

Speaking in terms of a single method, if one employs the means of "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to gather and transform others, one gradually leads them into the Buddha’s wisdom according to their actions. This is precisely the hook of gathering and transforming through common purpose.
This is the meaning of *artha*. To exhaustively give away whatever Dharma or wealth they seek, never feeling regret—this is the meaning of the "hook" (*aṅkuśa*) of conversion through giving (*dāna*).

To guide them with virtuous conduct and cause them to close the gates to the evil realms—this is the meaning of the "chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*) of conversion through beneficial action (*arthacaryā*). With unimpeded eloquence and skillful means...

To comply with this, one uses gentle words and affectionate speech to encourage and guide them, causing them to enter the Way. This is precisely the meaning of the bell that gathers and transforms through loving speech (*priyavāditā*).
Therefore, whenever the Buddhas abide in the world, they invariably transform sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).
Thus, the Verse of Dedication says: "May I realize the Unsurpassed Way and rescue those in the six realms by means of the four methods of attraction."
When the assembly recites the names of the Thirty-five Buddhas, they immediately appear in the lands of the ten directions, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.

From "Vairocana Buddha" to "Unsurpassed Wheel," the intent is to clarify that each of these Buddhas, within their respective lands, manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue to preach the Dharma.
Why is the Dharma called a "wheel"? A wheel possesses the qualities of pushing, crushing, and turning.

The meaning of "turning" (*vartana*) refers to turning this Dharma into the hearts of sentient beings, thereby shattering afflictions (*kleśa*), pulverizing ignorance (*avidyā*), transforming the ordinary into the sacred, and transporting them to the further shore of *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, it is said that "constantly turning" means preaching at all times, preaching at every moment, and preaching with fervent intensity; all of this is brought about by the original vow of Vairocana.
The assembly silently recites the Heart Sūtra once; this precisely accords with the intent of turning the wheel of Dharma.

As for the necessity of reciting the Heart Sūtra at this moment, it is because throughout the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the teachings, as well as the seventeen hundred koans, there is not one that does not desire people to directly realize this mind and penetrate this mind. To embody this is to be the Buddha. (From the *Śrī-siddhārtha-sūtra*)
It is said: "One who attains single-mindedness (ekacitta) shall extinguish the myriad evils. Furthermore, "mind" is a metaphor;
just as for a person's entire body, the mind is the sovereign, so too these six hundred rolls of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* are, in essence, the *Heart Sūtra*.
As it says: "Therefore, within emptiness, not only are the phenomena such as the five aggregates absent," and so forth.
The principles of the wisdom that takes the truths as its object are supramundane dharmas; within the true emptiness of the real mark (*dharmatā*), none of these can be apprehended.
Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed *nirvāṇa*, I would say it is like an illusion or a dream. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is like a great mass of fire.
Know that this sutra is the mother of all Buddhas and the source of the myriad practices. If one were to turn [the wheel of the Dharma]...

This Dharma can ferry one across the ocean of all suffering. If Bodhisattvas rely upon it for practice, they will be able to leave behind delusion, karma, and suffering, ultimately realizing non-abiding nirvana.
Because the Buddhas of the three periods of time relied on Prajñā, they attained unsurpassed bodhi.
Viewed in this light, escaping birth-and-death and entering nirvana proceeds by way of this path. How great is the mind!
Its light cannot be known by wisdom; its consciousness cannot be cognized. It is called the Great Divinity. It cannot be encompassed by yin and yang;
it is called the Great Illumination. There is nothing that can surpass it; it is called the Unsurpassed.
Not only can no phenomena equal it, but it can also equalize all phenomena, equalize all births, and [equalize] all...

It is equal, without high or low; it is called the "Unequaled-Equivalent Mantra. It can eliminate the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death and transform the basis into the secret treasury of the three virtues.
It is true and not false; furthermore, a secret mantra is spoken to assist in its manifestation.
There is this sublime benefit, which surpasses all other sutras. If there are those who hear the Dharma, not one among them shall fail to attain Buddhahood;
this refers to the fulfillment of the great vows previously made, namely that all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu* shall simultaneously attain Bodhi.
As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The body is the treasury of the True Dharma; the mind is the unobstructed lamp, illuminating and comprehending all phenomena."
"Emptiness is called 'delivering sentient beings.
This passage, from "I address the ten directions" to "immeasurable sages and worthies," is the primary narrative of the original intent of the food offering (*śrāddha*).
From its beginning to its end, it is divided into four sections; these six lines specifically constitute the invocation of the sages and worthies.
I, [Name], from this moment until [the end of the period], for the sake of all heterogenous spirits and deities, hereby express my own intent:
with a heart of compassion and relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, I invoke and summon the sentient beings of the six realms.

I only pray that all Buddhas will increase their compassion and protect me with mindful care. May these Buddhas and noble sages extend their great majestic light and, giving rise to hearts of pity and mercy, protect and mindfully care for me, so that my wishes may be fulfilled according to my heart’s desire.
"May all beings throughout the ten directions... realize the unsurpassed path. This is the formal expression of the vow for the offering of food as follows:
"I universally pray that all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, at this very moment, shall descend with certainty, riding upon the power of the Tathāgata."

Partaking of the nectar of the meal, may they give rise to the vast mind, leave behind the fruits of evil suffering, realize the unsurpassed path, and bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Hereafter, the five offerings shall be presented to complete the third offering.

[To all lands in the ten directions... until "...may they compassionately accept [me]. From the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* at the heart-center, light is emitted, producing six *hūṃ* syllables, each possessing a distinct color.
The flower is a pale red color; it symbolizes generosity (*dāna*), causing beings to give rise to joy. The incense is yellow;
it symbolizes ethical discipline (*śīla*), causing one's karmic conduct to become fragrant. The lamp is crimson; it symbolizes...
Patience transforms the fire of anger into a great radiance; its white color represents diligence, which moistens the Dharma-body.
Its fruit, red-yellow in color, represents meditative concentration, through which the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished. Its joy, green-blue in color, represents wisdom.
Because they are able to give birth to all manner of dharmas, these six Mother Goddesses take the six *pāramitās* as their essence.
Each has one face and four arms; the two upper hands each hold an offering, while the two lower hands cross at the wrists.

Possessing a graceful and beautiful countenance, they perform a dance posture with the left leg extended and the right knee bent, making offerings to all Buddhas. Interspersed between them is the Three-Syllable Mantra.
This refers to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all offerings, causing them to pervade as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

Regarding the phrase "the nature of causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-svabhāva*) up to *trima-ye hūṃ*: "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the respective seed-syllables; "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to their manifestation through external phenomena;

"nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to their arising from within, not existing externally. Furthermore, the recitation of the mantra and the binding of the mudrā are specifically distinguished [from the preceding].
In the Flower Garland (Huáfàn) tradition, this is clearly called "Er. Question: Is there such a celestial mother? Answer: This celestial mother exists within the central enclosure of Hevajra;
she is among the retinue of Buddhamātṛ, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra. She flows forth from the wisdom-activity of Vairocana and is included among the aforementioned thirty-seven deities.
Question: As for this... [smearing]... *Note: The final character "塗" (tú) appears to be an incomplete fragment of a question regarding ritual application.*
"What is it? [He] replied, "It is water. Why not simply call it "water," but instead say "coating"?
It is like the waters of the Ganges: fish and dragons see them as their dwelling place; devas and humans see them as lapis lazuli; those in the human realm see them as flowing waves;
and hungry ghosts see them as fierce fire. Originally it is but one water, yet what is seen differs for each. Therefore, names are taken [according to these perceptions].
They are also not the same. The person who can now make the offering is a celestial being; therefore, the water presented here is what they call *ārdra* (anointing water).
"By the power of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices" (up to) "I offer all these" is from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Extensive [Chapter on] Samantabhadra."
Cultivate offerings: universally pay homage and make offerings to all the sages and worthies throughout the dust-motes and lands of the universe.

Since you wish to cultivate these offerings, they must pervade the entire Dharma-realm like the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra; you must first mobilize your single mind, and only then will it be in accordance with the Dharma.
All the various offerings mentioned above are not yet offerings of the Dharma; it is only when you apply your mind that they truly become so.

This is the Dharma-offering. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Among all forms of offering, the Dharma-offering is supreme. Furthermore, the *Pratibhāna-pūrvayoga-parivarta* (The Chapter on Vows and Conduct) says:
"Even if one were to constantly offer various kinds of offerings to the Buddha, none would be as supreme as the Dharma-offering. As for the Dharma-offering:
This is precisely the bodhicitta. Why is this? Because the Tathāgatas honor the Dharma;
thus, if a bodhisattva practices the offering of the Dharma, its merit is beyond comparison. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"If one were to offer a single meal, a single garment, flowers, rice, necklaces, lamps, candles, banners, or flags to the Buddha—each such offering being as numerous as... [the sands of the Ganges].
One should study the Prajñāpāramitā before all Buddhas and their Saṃghas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This Prajñā is the Prajñā of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā);
it is the luminosity of the mind that is inherently possessed. As for the merit of making offerings, it resides in the mind and not in external things.
If one makes a single offering of food with a great resolve, one fully offers it to all Buddhas of the ten directions; one should not be hindered by distance or proximity.
