From this flows nectar (*amṛta*), silver-colored like mercury, produced by true wisdom (*jñāna*).
With the left hand, one sprinkles water empowered by the *bala-jñāna-bindu* (the drop of power and wisdom) into the void, causing it to fall like fine rain. Upon touching this water—
They all possess complete physical forms. The fierce fires are extinguished; they universally attain coolness and are freed from hunger and thirst. The karmic obstacles of the mind are eliminated.
You all, from immeasurable kalpas until now, have been free from all hindrances and difficulties. The fires of karma have already ceased, and you once again possess physical forms.

Although the signs [of attainment] appear, the throat remains ultimately unopened; therefore, you must open it for them. First, a verse is presented to correctly explain the cause of this obstruction:

"Since beginningless time, you have extensively created evil karma, giving rise to various forms of stinginess, greed, arrogance, deceit, and hypocrisy, as well as an empty stomach and a haughty mind. Due to such karmic actions, you have fallen..."
Hungry ghosts have vast bellies and narrow throats; thus, for thousands of millions of kalpas, they have not even heard the names of water or gruel.
Throughout the two periods of day and night, they suffer only the agony of fierce flames.

Now, by my recitation of this secret mantra, I cause your throats to become permeable and unobstructed, so that whatever food you receive shall attain the flavor of the Supreme Dharma, never again turning into pus, blood, iron dregs, or mire.

Furthermore, one should visualize that light rays emanate from the seed-syllable upon the moon-disc of the heart of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara within one’s own body, illuminating all sentient beings.
One should imagine that within the palm of the left hand there is a blue syllable *baṃ*, which transforms into a blue lotus flower.
Upon the flower is a white letter *A*, from which flows the water of nature, exceedingly cool and refreshing.

With his right hand, using the mudrā of patience and meditation, he sprinkles water into the void. Those sentient beings who come into contact with this water find their throats spontaneously opened, attaining unobstructed penetration;
they are thus able to produce sound and invoke the name of the Tathāgata. This section concludes the elimination of the obstacle of retribution.
Question: Previously, the syllable *hṛīḥ* was used for both [the body and speech]. Why, then, is the syllable *a* used here as well? Answer: The syllable *a* is the seed-syllable of speech;
therefore, it is employed according to the three original tantras.
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava... [until] all are completely extinguished.

Since their past karmic retributions have been exhausted, one should further recite the names of the seven Buddhas for them, causing them to hear the names and behold the forms, so that they may forever leave the ocean of suffering behind.

This refers to the meaning of ultimate, eternal bliss. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one merely hears the two characters for 'eternal-abiding' (*nitya*), one shall not fall into hell for seven lifetimes;
how much more so for the Tathāgata, who possesses ten thousand virtues? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Even if one hears the name of the Tathāgata and the Dharma he preaches but does not give rise to faith or understanding, it nevertheless perfumes the seeds [of enlightenment] such that one will naturally attain Buddhahood. It is like a person who eats but a small amount..."
*Vajra* (and so forth). Question: Do the Seven Buddhas possess distinctions of priority or inferiority? Answer: The Way of each Buddha is identical; there is no superiority or inferiority.
This refers to what is called the equality of speech, the equality of syllables, the equality of Dharma, and the equality of body.
As for their sequence of before and after, it is because each Buddha, while on the stage of practice (*bhūmi*), made great vows to benefit sentient beings; therefore, by means of these...
Their functions are set forth here: that which precedes is placed first, and that which follows is placed last.

First, because they have departed from the miserable realms yet the fires of their karma have not yet been extinguished, they must first rely on the name of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava so that it may be heard by them; this shall drench and extinguish the fires of their karma.
Upon hearing the name of this Buddha, they will be able to extinguish the fires of their afflictions (*kleśa*).

Homage to the Tathāgata Free from Fear (up to) Pure Bliss. Once the fires of karma have been extinguished, one finally leaves the realm of darkness and beholds for the first time the land of radiance. There, humans and devas gather together; ordinary beings and sages intermingle.
Since they do not exhibit an appearance of fear or terror, he next causes them to hear the name of the Tathāgata Free from Fear, so that upon hearing it,
they may forever be free from alarm and dread and always attain peace and happiness.
Homage to the Tathāgata Vipula-kāya (The One of Vast Body). [From this point] until attaining the flavor of ambrosia, all fear has ceased;

the constriction of the throat is forever pierced through. Therefore, one invokes the name of this Tathāgata so that those who hear it—upon hearing this majestic name just once—their obstructions shall open, the fires of karma shall be forever extinguished, and they shall attain clarity and coolness. The food they consume shall no longer transform into iron balls.
It is molten copper.
Homage to the Tathāgata Subhavarṇa (The One of Wondrous Form). [Up to: "He is the most supreme. Although he consumes ambrosia, his physical form remains thus without perishing.
One should invoke this Buddha’s name so that they may hear it. Upon hearing this great name but once, they shall immediately—

They shall no longer experience ugliness, but shall instead attain the perfection of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Only upon reaching this state will they be liberated from the forms of ghosts and animals.
Homage to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna... until their enjoyments become inexhaustible. Although they possess physical form, their attire may have been disheveled and their resources meager;
yet, by causing them to hear the name of the Tathāgata, they immediately attain a dignified and orderly appearance.
Their wealth and treasures will be abundant, fulfilling all their needs and desires.

Homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha... [until] entering the stage of non-retrogression. Having already attained what they wished for, yet fearing that faith among those in Jambudvīpa may be difficult to sustain, and further fearing that they may not always encounter the Buddhas to personally receive their teachings and make offerings, although—
Having received the transformative influence of the Dharma, it is difficult to fall back from the stage of non-retrogression;

therefore, by reciting the name of Amitābha, upon hearing that name even once, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, is born transformationally within a lotus flower, and enters the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
Homage to the Tathāgata Universal Sovereign Radiance of Vast Worldly Majesty (Namo Śrī-loka-vipula-tejovibhu-prabha-tathāgata). [Recite this] up to: "Like a lapis lazuli jewel.

Furthermore, those who invoke this name—namely, one who unifies all virtues in great completeness and illuminates the masses of darkness with singular brilliance—shall, upon hearing it but once, obtain five kinds of merit. Even if remaining in the world, they shall be the most honored among all in the world.
Just as when Siddhārtha was first born, he immediately declared: "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the Honored One.
Furthermore, he did not receive the body of an ordinary being; his marks and signs were upright and majestic, and his majestic virtue was vast and great.

Just as when a prince steps upon the ground, his nobility surpasses all ministers, so too does he possess the power of great sovereignty; wherever he turns, it is according to his will, and his flight is autonomous, free from all obstructions.
Furthermore, one attains a body as indestructible as a vajra and possesses the causes for great wisdom. Body and mind are transparently clear, like a lapis lazuli gem.
Without passing through the kalpas of the *saṃgha*, one suddenly awakens to the *dharmakāya*. Possessing such meanings as these, it may be said to be perfect in every way.
This concludes the extinction of afflictions.
"O sons of the Buddha... [to] the Unsurpassed Way. This is a general statement that the vows of the Tathāgatas of the seven Buddhas are vast and great;

they rescue sentient beings, causing them to leave suffering and attain happiness. If one recites their names even once, one can immediately leave suffering for a thousand lifetimes and realize the Unsurpassed Way.
The *Jiubai egui jing* (Sutra on Saving and Delivering Hungry Ghosts) says: The Buddha told Ānanda, "If a person desires to seek long life..."
One’s merit and prosperity will increase, and one will fulfill the dāna-pāramitā. At every dawn and at all times, take a single bowl and fill it with pure water;
place a small amount of rice, flour, cakes, and other foods therein, and press the vessel with the right hand.
To perform the rite of the Dharani of Immeasurable Majestic Virtue: recite the Mantra for Transforming Food twenty-one times.
Thereafter, invoke the names of the five Tathāgatas—namely, Ratnākara, Ratnaśrī, Suvarṇavarṇa, Abhayada, and Vipula-kāya.
Having invoked their names, snap your fingers seven times. At evening, take the food vessel and pour its contents into a clean place.
Having performed this offering, all the spirits and deities shall obtain full satisfaction. After casting off this body, they will surely be reborn in the heavens.

Such an offering is no different from one made to the Buddha; furthermore, its merit is increased because that Buddha, through the power of his vows, receives sentient beings and leads them to rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
It is especially emphasized during the two periods of the *xu* and *hai* hours. If one encounters these...
At such times, it is of no benefit for the matter at hand. Generally, those who observe the precepts and dwell in the mountains may also perform this rite to form karmic connections for future lives.
Every morning, fill an alms bowl with water and place it before the Buddha; recite the Great Compassion Mantra twenty-one times.
At noon, offer one vessel of food to the Buddha; recite the Mantra for Transforming Food twenty-one times. Upon reaching [the evening meal]...
In the evening, recite the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī twenty-one times and invoke the names of the Seven Tathāgatas. Thereafter, scatter the food.

Next, bestow the Three Refuges upon them, inspire the aspiration for Bodhicitta, and confer the Buddha-precepts. By thus offering the Dharma-food, one brings to completion the practitioner’s work of benefiting sentient beings.

Next, I shall lead you all to take refuge in the Three Jewels (up to) Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). By taking refuge in the Three Jewels, one can escape the three miserable realms (*trāya*).
After receiving [this refuge], you must protect it according to the Dharma, stay far away from deviant paths, and head straight for the shore of awakening; there is no other way to transcend them.
*Bokan* (婆龕) is also pronounced *Bokuken* (步欠), which signifies the meaning of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). This refers to what is called "the equality of all phenomena."
It is identical to empty space, being free from all material forms and obstructions. The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is markless; it is called the "true mark" because it is not a non-mark.
This implies the meaning of the Three Jewels as a single nature and a single essence. Next, one causes them to give rise to the bodhicitta. There are two meanings for "giving rise":
first, to open and develop; second, to manifest and reveal. The practitioner says it is "manifesting," while the assembly...
"Arising" should be understood as the manifestation of the originally existing awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). Therefore, the verse below states: "The awakened mind now manifested...
[omitting] ...the grasping at subject and object. This verse is the verse on the arousal of the mind from the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Six Perfections Sūtra).
"Awakened mind" is precisely the bodhicitta. Regarding "being far removed from intrinsic nature and characteristics," etc.:

If one relies upon the nature (*dharmatā*), then even in the state of equal quiescence there is no distinction between Buddhas and sentient beings; how, then, could there be such matters as seeking enlightenment above or transforming beings below?

If one arouses the mind based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is a fear of falling into the Two Vehicles. Characteristics involve birth and death, defilement and purity, and all manner of myriad differences.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind of birth and death as the fundamental cause for cultivation..."
To seek the Buddha-vehicle while [clinging to] birthlessness and deathlessness—this is impossible.

Because the characteristics of the world are, in essence, not permanent, one who resolves their mind based upon these fears falling into the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). To avoid these two faults, one does not rely upon them.

This extends even to not relying on the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve sense fields (*dhātu*), or the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); nor upon the grasper and the grasped, which are the delusions of mind and its objects.

The mind arises conditioned by karma, faculties, objects, and so forth; that is to say, it merely has a basis, being a mind of grasping and rejecting, arising and ceasing, rather than the non-abiding true mind.
Therefore, it is said that one must distance oneself from all attachments.
All phenomena are entirely without self (up to: because their emptiness is parinirvāṇa). Why must one depart from all phenomena?
Because all phenomena lack a real sovereign; they are primordially equal, just like space.
How could space, in turn, have anything upon which it depends? A sutra says: "Space has no basis. How, then, does one know that [phenomena] are like space?
It means that one's own mind is fundamentally unarisen from the beginning and does not perish now;
it is of a single mark which is markless, universally pure, and is called "nirvana by nature. It is empty and quiescent like space, and therefore space is taken as a metaphor for it.
This does not mean that space itself is the nature of nirvana. Why? Because space is a dull, insentient thing; how could it be compared to the numinous awareness [of the mind]?
This nature is luminous and not obscured; it is clearly and constantly aware. As the ancients said: "It is not like empty space;
its nature is inherently spiritual and understanding.
This refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (up to) "therefore, with a sincere heart, I pay homage. Since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas must necessarily rely upon Suchness...
They have resolved their minds upon the supreme Dharma; I now likewise resolve my mind upon it. For this reason, I prostrate with all my heart.
Next, I shall cause you all to resolve upon Bodhicitta; listen attentively. All Buddhas and I have all resolved upon this.
Mind. Therefore, you all should likewise rely upon this ritual method to take refuge in the Triple Gem and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "If you wish to see all Buddhas of the ten directions, and if you wish to bestow the inexhaustible treasury of merit..."
If you wish to extinguish the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, you should swiftly resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

Even if a glowing iron wheel [were to fall upon your head], [you should still resolve for] Bodhicitta. The preceding verses have served as an exhortation toward the further shore, desiring that they swiftly generate the Great Mind;
now, this section formally instructs them to vow to generate the Great Mind. Just as the World-Honored One generated Bodhicitta...
At that time, a powerful Māra king pressured the Buddha to submit. He said, "If you do not, I shall fly a wheel of glowing iron to crush your head to pieces.
The Buddha then made this vow: "Even if a wheel of glowing iron were to spin upon the crown of my head..."
"I shall never, for the sake of such suffering, retreat and lose the bodhicitta. When Māra heard this, he praised him, saying:
"The sun might be made cold, and the moon might be made hot, but the mind set on the unsurpassed path is difficult to turn back. If you attain Buddhahood, you should deliver me first;
therefore, I now borrow these verses to warn of the firmness of your resolve for the Way, lest you encounter circumstances and immediately retreat."
This is from the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness).
Next, one binds the Bodhicitta-mudrā. While reciting the mantra, one should contemplate that the Buddha, oneself, and sentient beings are non-different in the three aspects;
in a single thought-instant, they merge into one vast lunar disc, like the moon at midnight on an autumn night.
At a time when there are no clouds, it is exceedingly cool and brilliant, equal to empty space.
Within the lunar disc, one should visualize a golden letter *A*, as fine as the tip of an autumn hair—neither existent nor non-existent. At that moment:
One must not add anything to this thorough understanding. Above, there is no Buddha to be realized; below, there are no beings to be delivered;

in between, there are no practices to be cultivated. When afflictions and bodhi are seen as equal as flowers, and birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday—this is the great essential.
Students should apply their minds to this. Not only does it bring benefit to ghosts and spirits, but it also functions [as a practice].
Before long, those who understand this will also attain realization within it. Among the four kinds of nutriment, the meaning of the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is seen here.
Why? It refers to the awakening of the originally inherent enlightened nature of sentient beings, suddenly becoming identical with the wondrously luminous true nature of all Buddhas.
"Now for you all... (until) not being defiled or destroyed. You should know that this mind is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood.

The *Chapter on Vows and Practices* (*Pranidhānapatala*) says: "Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, take great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their essence, they give rise to great compassion because of sentient beings;
from great compassion arises the bodhicitta; and by means of the bodhicitta, they achieve [Buddhahood]."
Perfect Enlightenment. From the Three Refuges up to this point constitutes the breaking of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Why is this?

Because all afflictions are not necessarily subdued by mere discipline, nor are they destroyed except by wisdom. Once wisdom arises, all delusions are naturally eliminated, just as when light appears, darkness vanishes.
Now that the Great Mind has been generated, wisdom shall arise from this; once the Great Precepts are received, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) [will follow].
Arising from this, one becomes fully endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom. What concern could there be that ignorance and afflictions cannot be shattered?
This is what is called "severing delusions," and it is sufficient as proof.
Next, I shall confer upon you all the Samaya Precepts (up to the point where one) attains a share in the Buddha-dharma.

Having already generated the Great Mind as described above, you are now fit to receive the Samaya Precepts and enter the ranks of the Buddha’s sons. First, I shall recite the verses from the Brahmajāla Sūtra.

"You have received the Buddha’s precepts; these are the radiant Vajra Jewel Precepts. Once you have received these precepts, sentient beings who receive the Buddha’s precepts immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Having attained a rank equal to Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of all Buddhas."

Why is this? For their practice is identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual essence (*dharmadhātu*). Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One, the numinous marks of the ten bodies are fully perfected all at once;
how could they not be the children of the Buddha? This is precisely the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
The *Vajrasamaya Sūtra* states: "One who clearly awakens to the Buddha-nature is such a person that they do not maintain dualistic appearances.
Although they have not left the household life, they do not dwell in the household life; although they lack the Dharma-eye, they are not deficient in precepts.
By means of their own mind, they attain the fruit of sainthood without fail. The *Mahāyāna Sahasrapātra Mahātantra Sūtra* says: "Just as..."
The mind that arises is the vajra-nature; it is primordially pure and ultimately quiescent—this is called precept.
If one awakens to this essence of the precepts, all precious precepts will be spontaneously perfected, and one will suddenly enter the stage of the Tathāgata; this is named [the Precept Body].
He is a son of the Buddha. Next, as for binding the mudrā and reciting the mantra, this signifies equality, the removal of obstacles, and awakening.
The *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* states: "Just as upon entering the maṇḍala circle, one realizes samādhi;
all dharmas of meaning are fully possessed, and the three aggregates of pure precepts are simultaneously perfected. One should visualize the syllable *HŪṂ* in white within the mudrā."
He emits great rays of light that universally illuminate all sentient beings who are summoned.

Upon being touched by this light, the *śīla-pāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) of all Buddhas of the three times is simultaneously perfected. One visualizes the wholesome dharmas of the *dharmadhātu* as light;

its flowing radiance is poured over the crown of the head and stored within the body. The body becomes identical to the Universal Sage (*Samantabhadra*), seated upon a great lunar disc, and succeeds to the office of all Buddhas. As...
The Buddha’s legitimate son. Next, he joyfully exhorts Śāriputra with words of self-approval: "Precepts are the Dharma-body. One who awakens to this is as if newly born.
Furthermore, this is not a birth through the four modes of birth; rather, one is born from the mouth of the Tathāgata and is a transformation-born from the Dharma.
Once internal obstructions are purified, external appearances naturally become majestic. Moreover, one gives rise to the Great Mind..."
Only by receiving the Buddha’s precepts is one called a vessel of the Dharma, capable of receiving the food of the Dharma. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"Those who are equal regarding the Dharma are also equal regarding food. If one is not such a vessel, even if they receive ambrosia, it will instead turn into poison—just like lion's milk [in the stomach of a dog].
It must be stored in a lapis lazuli vessel; were it not for such a vessel, it would shatter.

Since you are called children of the Buddha, you should bestow upon them the food of the Dharma to nourish their Dharma-body and wisdom-life, so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall never be severed.
"O you sentient beings of both the living and the deceased, [this] offering of food mudrā and mantra can never be exhausted.
This very chapter of the mudrā and mantra was received by the Tathāgata from Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and transmitted to Ānanda;
it consists of only this single section. The preceding and following mudrās and mantras are all compiled by the Vajra Superior (Vajradhara) in accordance with the Yoga Tantra division."
This is the source from which the beginning and end of self-benefit and the benefit of others arise, thereby accomplishing the Buddha-activities of a single lifetime.
These mudrās and mantras are the spells and seals of the Tathāgata Infinite Majestic Virtue Sovereign Radiance (*Amitābha*).
Regarding this gate of contemplation, one must apply oneself with meticulous care; if one does not reach this point, all previously performed meritorious deeds will be rendered in vain.
One should use the right hand to perform the *tarjanī* (threatening) sprinkling. First, form the three-pointed mudrā and visualize a red syllable *HŪṂ* emitting light.
Recite "HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ" three times to dispel obstructing māras with the left hand. Question: What kind of māras are there in the hands?
Answer: This means that there are various types of microbes within the hands, and one should cause them to avoid [the offering].
Next, snap the fingers three times and recite "Oṃ Khaṃ. Visualize that the single syllable *Khaṃ* transforms into emptiness. Question: What is the meaning of "emptying the hands"? Answer:
It means that these hands are composed of the impure seeds of the father’s white element and the mother’s red element; therefore, they are now emptied. Furthermore, in a single moment of thought—
It transforms into hands of supreme and wondrous adornment, non-dual and indistinguishable from the Tathāgata’s *tūla-cotton* hands.
Question: Previously, having entered meditative absorption, one has already increased one's own body to become Avalokiteśvara; why, now, does one again dispatch the transformation of Māra into space?
Answer: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "After the World-Honored One had preached the *Ananta-artha*, he again entered *samādhi*."
He emitted light and proceeded to open the precious stupa; he again entered meditative concentration and emitted light. Is this not perhaps a case of confusion?
It is simply because one event manifests one particular dharma. It is like the worldly ritual: those who sacrifice in the ancestral temple do not fail to observe fasting and purification.

Furthermore, when it comes to the time of ascending the hall, one washes the hands once again. Why? It is said to signify reverence. Now, the demons are sent away once more and transformed into emptiness;
this signifies the depth of compassion, the extremity of pity, and the intensity of the mind’s application. Since they have been suddenly transformed:
Furthermore, visualize within the palm of your left hand a red syllable *baṃ*.
This transforms into a red lotus flower, upon which is a white syllable *vaṃ*, the secret lunar drop (*candramanī*). From within this, inexhaustible food and drink flow forth.
Furthermore, imagine that the water vessel before you is entirely made of Magadhan measures, adorned with the seven precious jewels, and filled to the brim with sweet [water].
Having displayed excellent and sublime food and drink, one should then visualize that the food transformed by this seed-syllable fills the entire *dharmadhātu*.
One recites "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hrīḥ hūṃ" one hundred and eight times. At that time, it is empowered and made vast.
Next, one recites the mantra for transforming food twenty-one times. With the two fingers—the *śīla* (purity) and *dhyāna* (meditation)—of the right hand, at...
From within the *bindu*, one takes the *amṛta* and sprinkles it into the void.

The attendant shall scatter the food upon the altar so that the ritual action (*事*) accords with the principle (*理*), ensuring that the meditative contemplation (*禪觀*) is not in vain. One *droṇa* of the kingdom of Magadha is equivalent to forty-nine *dǒu* of our own country.
What is called "a *droṇa* of food" refers to a wooden bucket-measure; "food" means rice. This is called the seventh [offering].
Regarding the number seven: seven grains can transform into seven *hu* (bushels); seven *hu* can transform into forty-nine *hu*.
Seven times seven again transforms them into the immeasurable Dharma-food of the ten directions. Therefore, it is called "food measured by the *hu*. Baiyun said:
"I have now performed the mantra and mudrā for you all; I shall transform this single meal into immeasurable food, as vast as Mount Sumeru."
Its measure is equal to the Dharma-realm; even if one were to exhaust an eon, it could not be depleted by taking from it, nor would it ever be exhausted by its use.
By the power of this mantra, [all beings] become fully satiated. Thus far, we have merely transformed various kinds of excellent and wondrous food and drink.

Fearing that they have not yet been fused into a single flavor and that they might be uneven, thereby exceeding the Buddha’s compassionate salvation, one should again recite this mantra of the Ocean of Milk.
By extending the power of this incantation, may all those foods be fused so that they become an ocean of milk, like various streams converging into a single taste.
May it be universally bestowed upon the hungry ghosts, causing their bodies and minds to be entirely satiated, so that they may enjoy it without end.
[It is] deficient. Question: Food can only nourish the body; how is it that the mind is also satiated? Answer:

It is said that this food is the *dharmāhāra* (Dharma-food). Food may sustain the body, but the Dharma can nourish the mind; this refers to the aforementioned meaning of *dharmaprīti* (joy in the Dharma) and so forth.
Again, seal the previous [mudrā]. When reciting the mantra, one should visualize nectar flowing from within the *bindu* of the syllable *vaṃ*. With the right hand...
He takes [a drop] and sprinkles it into the void; it falls like rain, and wherever it reaches, it immediately becomes a great river of ghee and curd.
Question: How can water from a small vessel pervade the entire Dharma-realm? Answer: Because the power of the mind is inconceivable.
Furthermore, this is augmented by the power of divine mantras, the visualization of seed-syllables (*bīja*), and even the secret empowerment of all Buddhas.
By the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), how could one not transform the small into the great and the few into the many?

For instance, when Luan Ba poured out a single cup of wine, by the power of his arts, he was still able to transform it into a drizzling rain; how much more so, then, the power of divine mantras (*śrutamantra*)!
A practitioner must therefore apply their mind diligently. During the Later Han dynasty, Luan Ba served as a Minister of the Interior (*shangshu*).
On the birthday of the Prince, the Sovereign bestowed wine upon him. [The Prince] sprayed it toward Shu. An official reported this as an act of irreverence.
Ba replied, "I was spraying the wine because Chengdu was on fire; I intended to extinguish it with it. Later, it was learned that Chengdu had indeed caught fire, and it was extinguished by rain.
There was the scent of wine within that rain; this was the matter. The *Zongjing Lu* states: "Because there is such greatness..."
The power of the wisdom of vows; the power of the self-nature of the dharma-realm being empty and devoid of intrinsic nature:
through these, all that is undertaken is spontaneously accomplished. Ordinary beings cling to them, their false views being narrow and obstructed.

If the barriers of attachment were absent, the myriad dharmas would follow one’s actions without departing from the realm of the single truth, manifesting in a hundred transformations of skillful means. Thus, the arrow piercing the stone tiger was not due to human effort.

O King, he is able to command immeasurable hosts of spirits; if their leader is raised up, the entire tribe follows.
"As numerous as the sands of the Ganges" is used here to illustrate the vastness of the number. This river is located in the Western Regions.
At the summit of Mount Gandhamādana, there is the Lake Anavatapta, from which four rivers flow. The Ganges flows to the south; it is forty *li* wide.
Sand flows with the water, as fine as flour. The Buddha often taught the Dharma here; this is raised as a metaphor for the five signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*).
When a Heavenly Lord is about to die, these signs of decay appear. There are distinctions between their magnitude.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: first, the flower crown withers and falls; second, sweat flows from beneath the armpits; third, the garments become soiled; fourth, the body...
The body emits a foul odor. Regarding the five signs of not delighting in one’s own seat, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: first, the fragrance of one’s clothing vanishes;
second, the radiance of the body suddenly extinguishes; third, bathing water adheres to the body; fourth, one’s natural disposition becomes restless and agitated; fifth, both eyes twitch.
These major manifestations signify certain death, whereas the minor ones are not fixed; they may be averted depending on circumstances.
The four marks: the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.

The four debts of gratitude: first, that of one's parents, for their compassionate care and nurturing; second, that of teachers and elders, for their instruction and the grace of wishing for one’s success;
third, that of kings, for the grace of governing with the True Dharma and providing for the land and its people; fourth, that of the Triple Gem, for the benefit and happiness [it provides].

Sentient beings are all alike in their debt of gratitude toward the Sangha, whether they be monastics or laypeople. If one can provide offerings and service, one will obtain immeasurable merit and will surely attain the Way of Buddhahood in the future.

The three realms of existence (*bhava*): the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These are the three worlds. That which does not forget cause and effect is called "existence.
The True Dharma of the Buddhas and the Sangha of Bodhisattvas are accomplished according to one's vows; this constitutes the second taking of refuge in the Triple Gem.
Previously, it was said that until the attainment of Bodhi, one vows to take refuge in the Triple Gem; now, it is said until [the end of cyclic existence].
I take refuge in Bodhi. From its source to its conclusion, there is nothing that does not rely upon the power of the Triple Gem; therefore, I dare not treat it with negligence.

Furthermore, I do not dedicate the roots of goodness I have cultivated solely for myself, but instead dedicate them so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may simultaneously attain Buddhahood.
Moreover, I pray that all mundane and supramundane dharmas will be accomplished in whatever place my aspirations lead. May it be so.
Ultimately, there shall be no obstacles whatsoever.
Relying strictly upon the *Yogācāra* teachings, [the ritual proceeds] until the seal is respectfully offered. Once the transformative rites are completed, one should universally offer the seal.

First, when performing the rite for realizing the three mysteries, one should visualize that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as those of the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, are present.

All these do not manifest. To speak in terms of investigating the ultimate principle, there is in reality neither coming nor going. If there were coming and going, how would this differ from ordinary worldly conditions?
If there were no welcoming or seeing off, the rites of propriety would not be fulfilled. This is because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is fundamentally without birth or extinction;

arising from the Truth (*tathatā*) to manifest transformation, he guides those with deluded faculties. Since the transformation is identical to the Truth, and the Truth and its response are of one limit, it is neither coming nor going.
Therefore, the *Vajra* [Sūtra] says: "It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere. Furthermore, transformation is itself the Real; fundamentally there is no coming or going.
Flowing forth as transformation from the Real, there is the appearance of departure and return. This is "coming with the aspect of not-coming," and "seeing with the aspect of not-seeing.
"Coming with the aspect of not-coming" is like the moon in water suddenly appearing; "seeing with the aspect of not-seeing" is likewise.
It is like the sudden appearance of flowers in the sky; it is like various illusory phenomena which, though devoid of coming or going, are clearly visible due to the power of illusion.
What I have now manifested is likewise so: by the power of the wisdom of my vows, the myriad phenomena are suddenly revealed.

Once the work of transformation is completed, how can the various marks remain? Since that which arises through conditions has no inherent nature, such is the nature of dharmas. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"All dharmas from the very beginning have always been characterized by quiescent extinction. Furthermore, it is like Sudhana visiting the rishi Viśvāmitra.
The immortal took his hand and immediately entered samādhi, wherein he fully beheld various matters such as subtle and wondrous adornments.
At that time, the immortal withdrew his supernormal powers, and in an instant, he was no longer visible; this is the proof thereof.

Next, recite the yakṣa verse: "O devas, asuras, yakṣas, and so forth. This verse is extracted from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-hṛdaya-mantra* (The Heart Sūtra of Dependent Origination), the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī*, and other scriptures.
By reciting this verse, one brings the fulfillment of virtuous retribution to completion.

Its intent is to exhort and admonish the Dharma-protecting deities, commanding them to protect the Dharma with sincerity, and to guard the nation and the people. Upon reaching this point, remove the five Buddha crowns.
Recite the mantra—the hundred-syllable mantra of Vajrasattva. This mantra is said to remedy deficiencies.
Should there be such faults as the hand gestures (mudrās) being out of order, the visualization lacking focus, or the mantras being mispronounced, one should recite [this mantra].

Having recited this mantra, all things become completely pure. Then, turning back to contemplate the golden letter *A* upon the moon-disc of one’s own mind, silently maintain it for twenty-one breaths. Thus, each of the previously mentioned acts of the perceiver and the perceived will be found to be ungraspable.
If it is not done in this way, one falls into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Question: When first entering the maṇḍala, then...
If the syllable *hṛīḥ* is the primary [seed-syllable], why should the syllable *a* be visualized here as well? Is it not the case that the primary focus differs between the beginning and the end?
Answer: The syllable *hṛīḥ* is the true essence of Great Compassion and the sublime wisdom for benefiting sentient beings; therefore, it is taken as the primary [syllable] at the outset.
The syllable *a* signifies non-arising (*anutpāda*) and is also called the "Bodhisattva’s Power of Entry into Non-differentiation."
Distinct realms. All that has been performed above is accomplished through the Illusion-like Samādhi:
sitting in meditation within a moon-in-water dharma-arena, subduing the demonic armies within a mirror, and performing the Buddha-work within a dream.

Although there are various distinctions, when sealed with the power of these syllables, their essential nature is likewise without distinction. Ultimately, one realizes and enters the self-nature of non-arising.
This is the nirvana of the nature (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, all that has been produced above arises from causes and conditions, yet the *dharmatā* is in reality without arising.

As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "All phenomena arise from conditions; they likewise cease from conditions. Phenomena arising from conditions do not arise; phenomena ceasing from conditions do not cease.
Within my own essence, how could there ever have been even a hair’s breadth of increase or decrease?
This is an abridgement. What is known as the *Yankou* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) is not something to be spoken of lightly.
From "I take refuge in the Triple Gem" (through to) "I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones," I again take refuge in the Triple Gem, requesting only that you bear witness.
Descend from your seat. Proceeding before the Buddha, recite the verse of dedication:
"The supreme practice of the merit of bestowing food... [up to] the pāramitās. This is the merit accumulated by this practitioner of the correct path.
Dedicate all of this in return for the sake of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, so that they may together be born in the Western Buddha-field of Immeasurable Life,
where they shall behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, enter the stage of non-retrogression, and realize the Unsurpassed Way.

Regarding the *Shishi Bu Zhu* (Supplementary Notes on the Offering of Food), the *Zhuchuang Suibi* (Random Notes from the Bamboo Window) states: "The teaching of the *Yankou Shishi* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts with Flames) was initiated by Ānanda;
it belongs to the Yoga Tantra class. The Yoga [Tantra] flourished greatly during the Tang dynasty through the two masters Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra."
They could command spirits and deities and shift mountains and seas; their majestic spiritual power was inconceivable.
After several generations, however, no one was able to succeed them; what remained was only the single method of offering food (*śrāddha*).
With hands forming mudrās, mouths reciting mantras, and minds performing visualizations—the coordination of these three karmas is called yoga—and this practice is by no means easy.
If even the mudrās and mantras are not necessarily refined now, how much more so the gate of contemplation? Thus, they would be inconsistent [with the goal].
Being inconsistent, not only would one be unable to benefit sentient beings, but one might even end up harming oneself.

Yesterday, a monk from outside the conventional world in the mountains was critically ill. That evening, while he was performing the rite of bestowing food (śatana-bhojana), he said to those tending him: "There is a ghost dragging..."
I went out with him to seek food, but he declined to go. After a short while, he returned and said, "The Dharma Master is not sincere; we shall return empty-handed.
We must certainly have some way to take our revenge. Thereupon, he took my arm and walked off together with me, while his followers carried poles, hooks, nets, and ropes.
When they attempted to drag this Dharma Master down to the ground, I was struck with great terror and cried out for help at the top of my voice;
at once, [the others] dispersed. Several days later, the monk died. It is because, before his death, he had already become the companion of these ghosts.
Had it not been for that cry of alarm, would the Master on the platform not have been in peril? This is not all; one monk who lacked sincerity was carried away by ghosts.
Upon reaching the riverbank, he intended to drown it. One monk had lost the lock to his robe-casket;

though he kept the key in mind, the various ghosts saw only iron shards upon the food and were thus unable to eat. Another monk was drying his felt robes and had not yet put them away when it began to rain.
He thought of this garment in his mind. When the hungry ghosts saw that the rice was entirely covered with animal fur, they were unable to eat it; thus, each received a manifest retribution.

Furthermore, one man entered the underworld and saw several hundred monks in a black room, their bodies emaciated and their complexions haggard, appearing as if they could not endure the weight of sorrow and suffering.
When he questioned them, they replied that they were all masters who had failed to provide food offerings. They bestowed [this teaching].
"Truly, eating is no easy matter indeed."
